Polyaniline as a conductive polymer and its role in improving the efficiency and conductivity of perovskite solar cells Valid Text Names: 'nazerian2608polyanilineasa pages 1-3', 'nazerian2608polyanilineasa pages 3-6', 'nazerian2608polyanilineasa pages 6-10', 'nazerian2608polyanilineasa pages 10-11', 'nazerian2608polyanilineasa pages 11-12', 'nazerian2608polyanilineasa pages 12-13' BibTex: @article{nazerian2608polyanilineasa, author = "Nazerian, Vahdat and Dizaj, Mehran Hosseinzadeh and Sutikno, Tole", title = "Polyaniline as a conductive polymer and its role in improving the efficiency and conductivity of perovskite solar cells", volume = "16", issn = "2722-256X", url = "https://doi.org/10.11591/ijpeds.v16.i4.pp2731-2743", doi = "10.11591/ijpeds.v16.i4.pp2731-2743", number = "4", journal = "International Journal of Power Electronics and Drive Systems (IJPEDS)", publisher = "Institute of Advanced Engineering and Science", year = "2608", month = "Dec", pages = "2731", issue = "4" } Abstract: This article investigates the role of polyaniline as a conductive polymer in the active layer of perovskite solar cells. Samples were created by incorporating polyaniline into the transport layers to assess its impact on enhancing efficiency and conductivity. The application of this polymer across various layers of the cell structure led to improved stability and performance. Given its high doping capability, polyaniline was examined in detail, particularly focusing on two types of oxidation doping and its integration into the hole transport layer. Graphene oxide and reduced graphene oxide were chosen as comparative models, and their performance was evaluated against the standard polyaniline configuration. Laboratory results revealed that power conversion efficiency increased by 17.5% with graphene oxide and by 36.8% with reduced graphene oxide. Furthermore, short-circuit current density improved by 9.8% and 23.1%, respectively. These findings are consistent with existing studies in the field and support the validity of the approach. Quantifying Perovskite Solar Cell Degradation via Machine Learning From Spatially Resolved Multimodal Luminescence Time Series Valid Text Names: 'barletta2026quantifyingperovskitesolar pages 1-2', 'barletta2026quantifyingperovskitesolar pages 2-4', 'barletta2026quantifyingperovskitesolar pages 4-6', 'barletta2026quantifyingperovskitesolar pages 6-7', 'barletta2026quantifyingperovskitesolar pages 7-9', 'barletta2026quantifyingperovskitesolar pages 9-11', 'barletta2026quantifyingperovskitesolar pages 11-12', 'barletta2026quantifyingperovskitesolar pages 12-14', 'barletta2026quantifyingperovskitesolar pages 14-16', 'barletta2026quantifyingperovskitesolar pages 16-18', 'barletta2026quantifyingperovskitesolar pages 18-20', 'barletta2026quantifyingperovskitesolar pages 20-21', 'barletta2026quantifyingperovskitesolar pages 21-22', 'barletta2026quantifyingperovskitesolar pages 22-23', 'barletta2026quantifyingperovskitesolar pages 23-24', 'barletta2026quantifyingperovskitesolar pages 24-29', 'barletta2026quantifyingperovskitesolar pages 29-33', 'barletta2026quantifyingperovskitesolar pages 33-35', 'barletta2026quantifyingperovskitesolar pages 35-35' BibTex: @misc{barletta2026quantifyingperovskitesolar, author = "Barletta, Giulio and Ternes, Simon and Ali, Saif and Abbas, Zohair and Ostendi, Chiara and D’Addio, Marialucia and Magliano, Erica and Asinari, Pietro and Chiavazzo, Eliodoro and Carlo, Aldo Di", title = "Quantifying Perovskite Solar Cell Degradation via Machine Learning From Spatially Resolved Multimodal Luminescence Time Series", year = "2026", journal = "Solar RRL", volume = "10", month = "Jul", doi = "10.1002/solr.70433", url = "https://doi.org/10.1002/solr.70433", publisher = "Wiley", issue = "15", issn = "2367-198X" } Abstract: Perovskite solar cells achieve remarkable power conversion efficiencies, yet operational stability remains a major barrier to large‐scale deployment. Reliable and rapid assessment of device state of health is therefore essential. Conventional electrical diagnostics, such as illuminated current–voltage (J–V) sweeps, provide accurate performance metrics but are time‐consuming and do not resolve spatially localized degradation, motivating non‐invasive imaging‐based alternatives. Here, a deep‐learning framework is introduced to estimate PSC efficiency retention, R PCE  = PCE t /PCE 0 , directly from multimodal luminescence imaging acquired during device aging. Each sample combines electroluminescence (EL), open‐circuit photoluminescence (PL oc ), and short‐circuit photoluminescence (PL sc ) at an aged state with device‐specific reference images at t  = 0, enabling learning of degradation‐relevant spatial changes. LumPerNet, a compact convolutional neural network, is benchmarked against a spatially homogenized control in which each luminescence channel is replaced by its spatial average while retaining the same learning framework and leakage‐aware protocol. The comparison indicates that global luminescence evolution contains most of the predictive signal, while spatial information provides a secondary contribution to robustness. These results establish spatially resolved luminescence imaging as a practical route for accelerated stability testing and non‐invasive degradation monitoring in perovskite photovoltaics. ## pqac-00000008

From text 'szymanski2024automatingthesynthesis pages 78-80'.

N Szymanski. Automating the synthesis and characterization of inorganic materials. Unknown journal, 2024.

The excerpt identifies the A-Lab’s robotic and automated handling equipment but does not provide glovebox brands, glovebox models, or details about how robot arms are mounted or powered inside a glovebox. The platform uses a bespoke precursor-preparation station equipped with a central Mitsubishi robot arm for powder dispensing and mixing. Two UR5e collaborative robot arms manufactured by Universal Robots transfer samples and labware between stations. One UR5e is specifically described as being mounted on a linear rail supplied by Olympus Controls, allowing it to remove dried samples and load them into downstream equipment. Powder dosing is performed with a Quantos automatic dispenser-balance from Mettler Toledo. Mixing uses a Smart DAC250 Dual Asymmetric Centrifuge from Hauschild, while liquid transfer is handled by an rLine LH-710969 automated pipettor from Sartorius. Other named equipment includes four box furnaces based on the F48055-60 Thermo Scientific model, with custom door actuators, and an Aeris Minerals powder X-ray diffractometer from Malvern Panalytical. The excerpt concerns the A-Lab specifically and does not describe comparable laboratories’ equipment or glovebox integration.

From text 'lisowski2026highthroughputsolidmicrosampling pages 15-18'.

Adam Lisowski, Henryk Żołnowski, Keyan Villat, Alec Schmidt, Edy Mariano, Jean-Charles Cousty, Jérôme Guérin, Ashley Stark, Frédéric Vasserot, Achim Ammon, David Gueller, Florian de Nanteuil, Jean-Jacques Schwartz, Mathias Cherbuin, Marc Kunze, Giuseppe Costanzo, and Pascal Miéville. This article has 0 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt identifies the automated robot used in the STORMS solid-microsampling system as a Universal Robots UR3e collaborative arm. It has six degrees of freedom, a 3 kg payload, 500 mm reach, and ±0.03 mm repeatability, making it suitable for operation in the confined glovebox environment. The arm is fitted with a Robotiq Hand-E gripper, specified with a 50 mm stroke, adjustable gripping force of 20–185 N, and approximately 0.025 mm repeatability; interchangeable fingertips handle different components. The text does not identify the glovebox manufacturer or model, nor does it describe the robot’s mounting arrangement, electrical/pneumatic power connections, or a separate commercial automated dosing system. Instead, dosing is performed through a vacuum-assisted solid coring module containing fixed and movable pneumatic grippers. The fixed gripper holds the outer steel tube, while the movable gripper holds the inner rod and provides 0–10 mm travel with 0.1 mm positioning resolution. The module is stationary to reduce vibration and unnecessary movement. Robot motions were restricted to limit airflow disturbance and vibration around the sampling module. Thus, this excerpt provides detailed robot and sampling-module specifications but no comparative information about A-Lab equipment or other autonomous solid-state synthesis laboratories.

The excerpt identifies the A-Lab GPSS as a robotic solid-state synthesis platform housed in a customized double-glovebox and operated under nitrogen in air-free conditions. It contains five integrated workstations for precursor powder dispensing, powder mixing, heating, post-heating grinding, and XRD sample preparation. Two robot arms are mounted on the glovebox floor and manipulate samples; a linear rail supports sample transfer. The platform also incorporates semi-automated powder XRD and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy workflows. XRD samples are manually sealed with Kapton films before being transferred outside the glovebox, while EIS samples remain inside the glovebox and are loaded into a custom test cell. However, these pages do not provide the robot manufacturers or model numbers, the specific automated dosing/dispensing equipment, glovebox brand or model, robot-arm payload/reach, mounting hardware details beyond floor mounting, or the electrical/pneumatic power arrangements inside the glovebox. They also contain no comparative equipment details for similar autonomous solid-state synthesis laboratories. It states that the nickel crucible and cap are commercially available: the crucible is from United Scientific Supplies (SKU NCR025), while the nickel-plated cap is repurposed from a Keystone Electronics steel hole plug (SKU 7610). The cap is friction-fitted into the crucible. For opening, a stationary gripper mounted in relation to the robot arm holds the crucible while the arm pulls the cap vertically from above. After each reaction, the cap is discarded; crucibles are manually removed for cleaning outside the glovebox, rinsed, scrubbed if necessary, and dried at 70 °C before reuse. Samples are stored in Parkway Plastic vials (SKUs A0430100PPC and C043C4SPTSW), with manually attached tracking labels. The excerpt references an “A-Lab GPSS synthesis workflow” video, but the supplied text contains no details about automated powder/liquid dosing equipment or the glovebox system. Chang’en Han, Xinghua Dong, Wang Zhang, Xiaoxia Huang, Linji Gong, and Chunjian Su. Intelligent systems for inorganic nanomaterial synthesis. Apr 2025. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/nano15080631, doi:10.3390/nano15080631. This article has 34 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt provides general equipment details for autonomous or automated inorganic nanomaterial synthesis, but it does not identify the specific robot-arm, dosing-system, or glovebox brands and models used in the A-Lab. One system uses a modular dual-arm robot housed in a tailored aluminum-profile enclosure. The robot interfaces with a liquid-handling station and an automated centrifuge, and a human–machine interface controls the system. Its modular architecture allows standard laboratory equipment and additional functional modules to be integrated for mixing, centrifugation, and customized synthesis workflows. The reported validation converted manual SiO2 nanoparticle synthesis into an automated process and demonstrated improved efficiency and reproducibility. A separate workstation based on the Symyx Technologies core module platform uses a liquid-handling robot, a heated needle for dispensing molten surfactants, a bottle fixture for solid handling, an automated balance, and an eight-reactor high-temperature array with independent temperature control and digitally adjustable stirring. For CdSe synthesis, the system operated in a nitrogen-filled glovebox, with the diffractometer outside. The excerpt does not describe how robot arms are mechanically mounted or electrically powered inside the glovebox, nor does it provide dosing-system or glovebox manufacturer/model numbers.

Abstract:
Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) promise an accelerated application of the scientific method. Through the automation of experimental workflows, along with autonomous experimental planning, SDLs hold the potential to greatly accelerate research in chemistry and materials discovery. This review provides an in-depth analysis of the state-of-the-art in SDL technology, its applications across various scientific disciplines, and the potential implications for research and industry. This review additionally provides an overview of the enabling technologies for SDLs, including their hardware, software, and integration with laboratory infrastructure. Most importantly, this review explores the diverse range of scientific domains where SDLs have made significant contributions, from drug discovery and materials science to genomics and chemistry. We provide a comprehensive review of existing real-world examples of SDLs, their different levels of automation, and the challenges and limitations associated with each domain.

Abstract:
The field of materials science stands at a critical inflection point. While laboratory innovations continue to emerge at an unprecedented pace, the traditional timeline from discovery to market in 10–20 years has become an unacceptable bottleneck in addressing urgent technological challenges. We argue that self-driving laboratories (SDLs) represent not merely another step in automation, but a fundamental reimagining of the materials development pipeline. By integrating manufacturing constraints and scalability considerations from the earliest stages of discovery, SDLs can collapse the laboratory-to-factory timeline while improving reproducibility and success rates. This requires abandoning the traditional sequential approach of materials screening, device optimization and manufacturing scale-up; in favor of concurrent cross-scale development. Here, we critically examine current SDL implementations, challenge prevailing assumptions about automation in materials science, and propose a roadmap for truly integrated materials development platforms that could revolutionize how we translate laboratory discoveries into commercial products.

Abstract:
<jats:p>This review proposes the concept of a “frugal twin,” similar to a digital twin, but for physical experiments. Frugal twins range from simple toy examples to low-cost surrogates of high-cost research. For example, a color-mixing self-driving laboratory (SDL) is a low-cost version of a costly multi-step chemical discovery SDL. We need frugal twins because they provide hands-on experience, a test bed for software prototyping (e.g., optimization, data infrastructure), and a low barrier to entry for democratizing SDLs. However, there is room for improvement. The true value of frugal twins can be realized in three core areas. Firstly, hardware and software modularity, secondly, purpose-built design (human-inspired vs. hardware-centric vs. human-in-the-loop), and thirdly state-of-the-art (SOTA) software (e.g., multi-fidelity optimization). We also describe the ethical benefits and risks that come with the democratization of science through frugal twins. In future work, we suggest ideas for new frugal twins, SDL educational course outcomes, and a classification scheme for autonomy levels.</jats:p>

## pqac-00000013

From text 'leong2025steeringtowardssafe pages 30-33'.

Shi Xuan Leong, Caleb E. Griesbach, Rui Zhang, Kourosh Darvish, Yuchi Zhao, Abhijoy Mandal, Yunheng Zou, Han Hao, Varinia Bernales, and Alán Aspuru-Guzik. Steering towards safe self-driving laboratories. Dec 2025. URL: https://doi.org/10.26434/chemrxiv-2024-2qx28, doi:10.26434/chemrxiv-2024-2qx28. This article has 81 citations.

The excerpt provides prospective design lessons for self-driving laboratories (SDLs) operating in gloveboxes, rather than reporting a detailed operational postmortem with quantified downtime or maintenance records. Constrained glovebox spaces make robotic-arm collisions more likely, so complex workflows require substantially better motion planning and spatial optimization. The text implies that systems designed for individual operations, such as liquid handling or solid weighing, may not readily scale to complete automated workflows. A further burden is that many robotic systems lack cleanroom certification; consequently, their long-term maintenance and safety in oxygen- and moisture-free environments require additional analysis. For air- and moisture-sensitive materials, the SDL must preserve inert conditions through measures such as global purging, inert-gas blankets, adapted apparatus, or robotic systems installed inside inert gloveboxes. Air or moisture ingress can quench sensitive reagents, clog tubing, corrode hardware, and, for pyrophoric compounds, cause fires or explosions. The cited example, the “Schlenkputer,” demonstrates autonomous control of Schlenk-line valves and vacuum for sensitive syntheses, but the authors characterize this area as nascent. Thus, the practical “do differently” guidance is to design safety, inert-atmosphere control, collision avoidance, maintainability, certification, and spatial planning into the SDL from the beginning. Specific downtime causes and explicit author recommendations based on prior operations are not reported in this excerpt.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) are major drivers in on-site power generation for smart devices, enable self-powered sensors, and introduce novel catalytic processes. Here, we demonstrate adamantane plasma polymers as versatile dual-polarity triboelectric surfaces capable of exhibiting either tribopositive or tribonegative behavior through simple control of the plasma deposition configuration, without additives or post-functionalization. By modifying the substrate orientation relative to the plasma, thin-film polymers with distinct dielectric, mechanical, secondary electron emission, and triboelectric properties are obtained. The high conformality, stability, and processability of the polymers enable their direct implementation into solid-solid, solid-liquid, and hybrid piezo-triboelectric configurations. Additional surface texturization through buckling provides voltage and current outputs as high as 90 Vpeak-to-peak and 0.6 µA cm-2 for a 2.8 µm (tribonegative) vs. 400 nm (tribopositive) combination with a maximum mean power density of 2.1 µW cm-2. A maximum peak power of 200 µW is generated from salty droplets in drop-TENG configuration employing a 500 nm-thick tribopositive adamantane polymer. These layers sustain more than 105 cycles in solid-solid nanogenerators and 104 droplet impacts in solid-liquid devices. Combined with an environmentally friendly and industrially scalable synthesis route, these results position adamantane plasma polymers as a robust and versatile platform for next-generation triboelectric energy-harvesting materials.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Tribology at cryogenic temperatures has attracted much attention since the 1950s with the acceleration of its applications in high-tech equipment such as cryogenic wind tunnels, liquid fuel rockets, space infrared telescopes, superconducting devices, and planetary exploration, which require solid lubrication for moving parts at low temperatures down to 4 K in cryogenic liquid, gaseous, or vacuum environments. Herein, the research progress regarding cryo-tribology is reviewed. The tribological properties and mechanisms of solid lubricants listed as carbon materials, molybdenum disulfide, polymers, and polymer-based composites with decreasing temperature are summarized. The friction coefficient increases with decreasing temperature induced by thermally activated processes. The mechanism of transfer film formation should be considered as a significant way to enhance the tribological properties of solid lubricants. In addition, applications of solid lubrication on moving parts under cryogenic conditions, such as spherical plain bearings and roller bearings, are introduced. The technology for tribological testing of materials and bearings at cryogenic temperatures is summarized, where the environmental control, motion and loading realization, as well as friction and wear measurement together in a low-temperature environment, result in the difficulties and challenges of the low-temperature tribotester. In particular, novel technologies and tribotesters have been developed for tribotests and tribological studies of solid lubricants, spherical plain bearings, and roller bearings, overcoming limitations regarding cooling in vacuum and resolution of friction measurement, among others, and concentrating on in-situ observation of friction interface. These not only promote a deep understanding of friction and wear mechanism at low temperatures, but also provide insights into the performance of moving parts or components in cryogenic applications.

Abstract:
Just as geological samples from Earth record the natural history of our planet, astromaterials hold the natural history of our solar system and beyond. Astromaterials acquisition and curation practices have direct consequences on the contamination levels of astromaterials and hence the types of questions that can be answered about our solar system and the degree of precision that can be expected of those answers. Advanced curation was developed as a cross-disciplinary field to improve curation and acquisition practices in existing astromaterials collections and for future sample return activities, including meteorite and cosmic dust samples that are collected on Earth. These goals are accomplished through research and development of new innovative technologies and techniques for sample collection, handling, characterization, analysis, and curation of astromaterials. In this contribution, we discuss five broad topics in advanced curation that are critical to improving sample acquisition and curation practices, including (1) best practices for monitoring and testing of curation infrastructure for inorganic, organic, and biological contamination; (2) requirements for storage, processing, and sample handling capabilities for future sample return missions, along with recent progress in these areas; (3) advancements and improvements in astromaterials acquisition capabilities on Earth (i.e., the collection of meteorites and cosmic dust); (4) the importance of contamination knowledge strategies for maximizing the science returns of sample-return missions; and (5) best practices and emerging capabilities for the basic characterization and preliminary examination of astromaterials. The primary result of advanced curation research is to both reduce and quantify contamination of astromaterials and preserve the scientific integrity of all samples from mission inception to secure delivery of samples to Earth-based laboratories for in-depth scientific analysis. Advanced curation serves as an important science-enabling activity, and the collective lessons learned from previous spacecraft missions and the results of advanced curation research will work in tandem to feed forward into better spacecraft designs and enable more stringent requirements for future sample return missions and Earth-based sample acquisition.

               Nonetheless, the creation of laboratory digital twins would require advanced modelling

            techniques that can account for numerous variables, many of which may be unknown or

         3.2  Strengthening the SDL safety ecosystem


           When implemented effectively, SDLs can empower various workflows and democratize

             access to cutting-edge hardware, personnel and software systems181. However, this broad

           range of capabilities comes with many risks to all parties involved, such as damaging lab

              assets, contaminating experiments, or even injuring ground personnel and scientists. Hence,

           a robust ecosystem for the safe design and deployment of SDLs is crucial to realize their

             capabilities while mitigating these risks fully.


            3.2.1  Workforce training

              Reports by the American Chemical Society182,183 and the National Research Council

              of the National Academies of Science184 have emphasized that a strong safety culture and

            robust safety skills are essential to prevent devastating accidents in traditional laboratories,

          and we are of the opinion that the same holds true for SDLs.

            Compared to traditional labs, SDLs incorporate a larger number of moving parts, in-

            cluding robots and mobile stations, which introduces a different kind of risk to personnel

           working in proximity185. Although existing chemical safety protocols including wearing the

            hoods187, and implementing spill and emergency management188 remain relevant, specialized

             training is essential for personnel working in shared spaces of human-robot. As highlighted

             in a recently concluded workshop on Accelerated Materials Experimentation Enabled by the

          Autonomous Materials Innovation Infrastructure (AMII) in support of the 2021 Materials

         Genome Initiative (MGI) Strategic Plan189, a common gap across materials domains relates

            to safety and safe use. In addition to the hardware-based safety nets discussed in the pre-

            vious sections, it is thus crucial to educate personnel about safe maintenance protocols and

           emergency stopping procedures for different levels of severity in the form of safety-rated

           monitored stops190.  More workforce training is also vital to establish a critical mass of

             qualified workforce with expertise not only in experimental science, AI/ML, and automa-

             tion technologies189 but also in the safety practices necessary to operate within these SDL

            environments.

              However, we acknowledge that the rarity of safety incidents can lead to complacency over

            time, making it difficult to sustain the high level of readiness and competency required for

              effective responses in real life191. Furthermore, as SDLs continue to evolve, the continuous

            adaptation of safety protocols becomes inevitable, necessitating ongoing safety training and

            workforce engagement to ensure personnel are always well-equipped.


            3.2.2  SDL safety level classification


                Different SDLs are built to handle different capabilities, making some inherently more

           hazardous than others. For example, SDLs handling shock-sensitive substances will require

           a different set of safety features than those handling corrosive chemicals due to the varying

            nature of the interaction of the substances with equipment187. This calls for the need to

             categorize SDLs depending on their functions and risk levels, thereby creating a framework

              for defining requirements, best practices, and appropriate protocols tailored for each category.

            One possible way to implement this would be a system inspired by the Biosafety levels



                                                  27



https://doi.org/10.26434/chemrxiv-2024-2qx28 ORCID: https://orcid.org/0000-0001-8130-0897 Content not peer-reviewed by ChemRxiv. License: CC BY-NC 4.0           (BSLs) used in biology laboratories192. These consist of 4 levels defined by the nature of the

             biological agent being studied, each with specific guidelines and best practices to ensure the

            appropriate containment level. Similarly, the classification of SDL risk could be structured

           around a set of three key risk factors, namely the level of autonomy of SDL53, the likelihood

              of accidents and the severity of accidents. The level of autonomy affects the type and scale

              of damage during an accident. SDLs with a higher percentage of collaborative spaces could

           have a higher risk of human injury, while more autonomous SDLs could risk greater damage

            to property due to the larger scale of experiments. The likelihood of accidents is directly

            influenced by the nature of the SDLs (type of materials and substances being handled)

          and by the efficacy of autonomous systems. The severity indicates the potential harm to

         human life (personnel and otherwise), assets, and environmental impacts. A hypothetical

           implementation of such a framework is outlined in Figure 4. We advocate for active dialogue

            within the SDL community to collaboratively define a unified risk assessment matrix to

              facilitate the development of effective safety regulations and protocols. Given the rapid pace

              of SDL development, this matrix should remain dynamic to incorporate updates based on

             further technological advancements and emerging risks.

            3.2.3  Governing bodies and collaboration between stakeholders


              Governing bodies are crucial in establishing a strong foundation to build safe SDLs by

              facilitating collaboration among various stakeholders such as academics, industry experts,

             researchers, and regulatory agencies. They are also important for defining and enforcing pro-

              tocols, as well as in certifying compliance and safety standards193. These collaborative efforts

              will create safer environments for SDLs, ultimately advancing chemical safety practices.

          We see examples of such bodies in the development of biosafety protocols for biology labo-

             ratories by the World Health Organization (WHO), those for “Robots and robotic devices —

            Collaborative robots” defined in ISO 15066:2016, and those for aviation by the Civil Aviation

           Authority (CAA) and International Air Transport Association (IATA). These organizations

             also investigate accidents and make recommendations and amendments to operating proce-

             dures, significantly enhancing the safety ecosystem within their respective fields193. These

             existing practices serve as excellent guidelines and recommendations for developing compre-

            hensive regulatory frameworks and best practices to ensure safety in SDLs.  Additionally,

## 5. szymanski2024automatingthesynthesis pages 76-78 (Context ID: pqac-00000023)

d synthesis routes are designed using two hypotheses: 1) solid-state reactions
tend to occur between two phases at a time (i.e., pairwise)84; and 2) intermediate phases that leave
only a small driving force to form the target material should be avoided, as they often require long
reaction time and high temperature89,90.
      The A-Lab continuously builds a database of pairwise reactions observed in its experiments
– 88 unique pairwise reactions were identified from the synthesis experiments performed in this
work. This database allows the products of some recipes to be inferred (Figure 5-3), precluding
their testing; a recipe that yields an observed set of intermediates (already present in the lab’s
database) need not be pursued at higher temperatures, as the remaining reaction pathway is already
known. This can reduce the search space of possible synthesis recipes by up to 80% when many
precursor sets react to form the same intermediates (Figure 5-3e). Furthermore, knowledge of
reaction pathways can be used to prioritize intermediates with a large driving force to form the
target, computed using formation energies available in the Materials Project. For example, the
synthesis of CaFe2P2O9 was optimized by avoiding the formation of FePO4 and Ca3(PO4)2, which
have a small driving force (8 meV/atom) to form the target. This led to the identification of an
alternative synthesis route that forms CaFe3P3O13 as an intermediate, from which there remains a
much larger driving force (77 meV/atom) to react with CaO and form CaFe2P2O9, causing a ~70%
increase in the target’s yield.

5.2.3 Barriers to synthesis
Seventeen of the 58 targets evaluated by the A-Lab were not obtained even after its active learning
cycle. We identify slow reaction kinetics, precursor volatility, amorphization, and computational
inaccuracy as four broad categories of “failure modes” that prevented the synthesis of these targets.
The prevalence of each failure mode is shown in Figure 5-4, accompanied by their affected targets.
       Sluggish reaction kinetics hindered 11 of the 17 failed targets, each containing reaction
steps with low driving forces (< 50 meV/atom). In principle, these targets can be made accessible
by using a higher synthesis temperature, longer heating time, improved precursor mixing, or
intermittent regrinding – standard procedures that are currently outside the domain of the A-Lab’s
active learning algorithm. As such, we manually reground the original synthesis products
generated by the A-Lab and heated them to higher temperatures, which led to the successful
formation of two additional targets, Y3Ga3In2O12 and Mg3NiO4, bringing our total success rate to
74%. One could also use more reactive precursors to provide a greater driving force to form the
target; though, our experiments were constrained to air-stable binary precursors that sometimes
restricted the A-Lab’s choice of synthesis routes to those forming highly stable intermediates.
System modifications to enable multi-step heating, intermediate regrinding, and expanded
precursor selection should improve the lab’s ability to adapt and overcome failed synthesis
attempts.
       Precursor volatility disrupted all synthesis experiments targeting CaCr2P2O9, causing a
change in the net stoichiometry of its samples. This can be attributed to the use of ammonium
phosphate  precursors, NH4H2PO4 and (NH4)2HPO4, which  proceed  through  a  series  of
decomposition reactions and ultimately evaporate above 450 °C152. Still, recipes based on these
precursors can succeed if the ammonium phosphate reacts with another precursor prior to its
evaporation temperature, effectively locking the phosphate ions in the solid state. For example,

                                      67volatility does not appear to be an issue for the Mn-containing phosphates targeted in this work,
as each Mn oxides precursor reacts with the ammonium phosphates at low temperature (< 500 °C)
to form Mn2(PO4)3 as an intermediate. This precursor behavior can in principle be learned when
sufficient pairwise reaction data has been collected, after which the A-Lab may favor the selection
of precursors that trap in phosphate ions at low temperature and therefore preclude unwanted
volatility.
       Melting of samples  at high temperature inhibited the  crystallization of one  target,
Mo(PO3)5, whose synthesis attempts produced amorphous samples. While the use of a molten flux
can sometimes improve reaction kinetics153, the formation of an amorphous state that is low in
energy may reduce the driving force for crystallization. Indeed, using the workflow outlined by
Aykol et al.154, we identified amorphous configurations of Mo(PO3)5 with energies as low as 61
meV/atom above the crystalline ground state, a finding that is consistent with the widely reported
glass-forming ability of phosphate-rich compounds155,156.

5.3 Discussion
In 17 days of closed-loop operation, the A-Lab performed 355 experiments and successfully
realized 41 of 58 compounds with diverse structures and chemistries. This unexpectedly high
success rate (71%) for the synthesis of computationally predicted compounds was achieved by
integrating robotics with 1) DFT-computed data to survey the energetic landscape of precursors,
reaction intermediates, and final products; 2) heuristic suggestions for synthesis procedures
obtained from ML models trained on text-mined synthesis data; 3) ML  interpretation of
experimental data; and 4) an active learning algorithm that improves upon failed synthesis
procedures. The study also revealed several opportunities to enhance the lab’s active learning
algorithm by addressing failures caused by slow reaction kinetics, which would enable an
improved success rate of 74% with in-line solutions.
      Our paper demonstrates that autonomous research agents can dramatically accelerate the
pace of materials research. Researchers initialized the A-Lab by proposing 58 target materials,
which were successfully realized at a rate of > 2 new materials per day with minimal human
intervention. Such rapid discovery points to a vast landscape of opportunities in materials synthesis
and development. While the current work focused on a limited subset of all possible synthesis
targets, many new candidates await evaluation. As the breadth of ab-initio computations continues
to grow, so will this list of novel materials.
      Advances in simulations, ML, and robotics have intersected to enable “expert systems”
that display autonomy as an emergent quality by the sum of its automated components. The A-Lab
demonstrates this by combining modern theory- and data-driven ML techniques with a modular

5.4 Methods

5.4.1 Materials screening
The 58 targets evaluated by the A-Lab were identified from the Materials Project database (version
2022.10.28). We  first obtained  all entries from the Materials Project that were marked as
“theoretical” (i.e., not represented in the ICSD) and predicted to be thermodynamically stable (at
0 K) or very close to the convex hull (< 10 meV/atom). We did not consider materials with ≤ 2
elements, nor those containing elements that are radioactive (Ac, Th, Pa, U, Np, Pu, Tc),
exceedingly rare (Pd, Pt, Rh, Ir, Au, Ru, Os, Re, Tl, Sc, Tm, Pm, Rb, Cs), or toxic (Hg, As). Due
to concerns with the experimental handling of certain material systems (e.g., sulfides), we
constrained our selection to only include the following types of materials: oxides, carbonates,
bicarbonates, hydroxides, sulfates, sulfites, bisulfates, silicates, fluorides, chlorides, bromides,
orthoborates,  metaborates,  tetraborates,  phosphates,  phosphites,  chlorates,  chlorites,  and
hypochlorites. Finally, we removed all compounds predicted to have uncommon and potentially
challenging oxidation states (e.g., Co4+), as determined by pymatgen63.
      The novelty of each candidate material was verified by cross-checking with several
experimental sources. We first removed all compositions that appeared in SynTERRA, a text-
mined set of experimental synthesis data extracted from more than 24,000 publications160.
Additionally, we removed any materials with compositions appearing in the Handbook of
Inorganic Substances (de Gruyter)161. While these methods are not exhaustive, they provide an
automated and high-throughput approach to screen for materials novelty. For the remaining 432
candidates that were labeled as previously unsynthesized using this workflow, we filtered by
thermodynamic stability in air. This was done by calculating the formation energy of each
compound in a grand potential with respect to oxygen, assuming standard atmospheric conditions
(pO2 = 21,200 Pa) and temperatures ranging from 600-1100 °C. We further checked for reactivity
with CO2 and H2O under those same conditions by using the Interface Reactions module in
pymatgen. From the resulting list of 146 new compounds that were stable in air, we selected 58
targets for which precursors were readily available.
      The algorithm we used for identifying potential synthesis targets is available on GitHub
(github.com/mattmcdermott/novel-materials-screening). It operates autonomously once given the
following information: which elements to consider in the target materials, how large an upper limit
to impose on each material’s energy above the convex hull, the atmospheric conditions under
which the materials will be synthesized, and a threshold on the reaction energies that exist between
each material and the gaseous species present in the specified atmosphere. The algorithm then
scrapes the Materials Project and produces a list of candidate materials that satisfy these criteria.
Additional filtering may be considered based on the availability and cost of precursors for each
target. While this is done manually in the current version of the algorithm, potential improvements
could automate the process by leveraging online data from chemical inventory lists and vendor
websites.




                                      705.4.2 Synthesis recipes from text-mined knowledge
We have established a pipeline for recommending synthesis recipes by using a knowledge base of
33,343 solid-state synthesis procedures extracted from 24,304 publications160. For a given target,
the initial recipe is selected based on the most common precursors in the knowledge base. We then
transition to a similarity-based strategy for recipe selection100,151. Each target is transformed into a
numerical vector by using a synthesis context-based encoding model. The similarity between a
given (new) target and each known material in the knowledge base is evaluated using the cosine
similarity between their encoded vectors. After identifying the reference material that is most
similar to the target, its precursors are included in the new recommendation. When these precursors
do not cover all the elements in the target, we use a masked precursor completion model to account
for such missing precursors. Subsequent recommendations are implemented by moving down the
list of known materials ranked to be most similar to the target.
      For each set of recommended precursors, the most effective synthesis temperature is
predicted using an XGBoost regressor trained in previous work99. The target and its associated
precursors are transformed into three sets of features: (1) precursor properties including melting
points, standard enthalpies of formation, and standard Gibbs free energies of formation; (2) target
compositional  features  indicating  which  elements  are  present;  and  (3)  the  calculated
thermodynamic driving force associated with pairwise reaction paths from precursors to target.
While the proposed synthesis temperature is dependent on the precursors, not just the target, it may
vary for each recipe. However, to maximize the efficiency with which the A-Lab operates, we
chose to use one fixed temperature for each target. This temperature was calculated by averaging
the proposed synthesis temperatures for the top five precursor sets recommended for a given target.
This allowed all such precursor sets to be batched in a single furnace.

5.4.3 Robotic synthesis & characterization
The A-Lab performs fully automated solid-state synthesis and characterization. It is a bespoke
robotic platform that consists of a precursor preparation station with a central robot arm
(Mitsubishi) for powder dispensing and mixing (custom-made with Labman Automation Ltd.), a
high-temperature heating station with four box furnaces (based on F48055-60, Thermo Scientific
with custom actuators to control its door), a product handling station developed in-house for
powder retrieval and sample loading, a characterization station with a powder X-ray diffractometer
(Aeris Minerals, Malvern Panalytical), and two collaborative robot arms (UR5e, Universal Robots)
that transfer samples and labware between stations.
      The synthesis process starts from the precursor preparation station, where the necessary
consumables (plastic vials, ZrO2 balls, and crucibles) and precursor dosing bottles containing
between 50 and 100 g of powders are manually loaded prior to starting a new experimental
campaign. Prescribed amounts of the precursor powders are dispensed into a plastic vial by an
automatic dispenser-balance (Quantos, Mettler Toledo). The precursor powders are then mixed
thoroughly with ethanol and ten 5 mm ZrO2 balls in a Dual Asymmetric Centrifuge (Smart
DAC250, Hauschild) for 9 minutes. To ensure proper slurry viscosity, the ethanol amount is
automatically calculated based on the amount and density of each powder comprising the mixture.
The resulting slurry is transferred with an automated pipettor (rLine LH-710969, Sartorius) into
an alumina crucible, which is then dried at 80 °C in a closed evaporation system. A UR5e robot
arm on a linear rail (Olympus Controls) removes the dried samples from the precursor preparation

The hot injection technique for the synthesis of quantum dots (QDs) is a well-established and

widely used method in the lab. However, scale-up rules do not exist. One reason is that in

particular the role of process parameters like mixing on particle formation is largely unknown, as

systematic examination of the  latter  is impossible for the laborious and complex manual

synthesis. Herein we studied the mixing induced self-focusing of particle size distributions

(PSDs) of CdSe QDs using automation in combination with a defined stirrer geometry. Basis for

our study is a platform that allows parallelization with inline temperature monitoring, defined

                                      1injection rate, accurate sampling times as well as controlled stirring. Reproducibility in terms of

optical product properties was analyzed by absorption and emission whereas reproducibility in

terms of the PSD was verified by deconvolution of UV/Vis absorbance spectra and especially by

analytical ultracentrifugation (AUC) complemented by transmission electron microscopy. In line

with previous results, AUC confirmed that even QDs made by hot injection in an automated

setup are polydisperse with multimodal size distributions. Finally, reproducibility in combination

with early stage sampling and controlled mixing allowed us for the first time to analyze the

influence of stirring on focusing and defocusing of PSDs, that has been expressed in terms of

the evolution of the relative standard deviation (RSD). Our work paves the way to gain in-depth

understanding of often forgotten process-structure relationships of colloidal nanoparticles which

eventually is a first step in the direction of the development of scalable synthesis and reliable

application of high-quality QDs in technical applications.

1 Introduction

Although hot injection is a widely used technique for the preparation of quantum confined

semiconductor nanoparticles (usually referred to as quantum dots (QDs)),[1] with manifold

applications  in the fields of energy,[2-4] biology,[5-7] telecommunication,[8, 9] and display

technology,[10-13] design rules for scalable processes for this complex kind of synthesis do not

exist. This originates from an insufficient understanding of the underlying particle formation

dynamics in combination with even less knowledge on the role of process parameters that finally

prevents the design of appropriate equipment, unit operations and processes. Several aspects

can be identified why this is so: (i) ill-defined mixing due to the nearly exclusive use of small-

volume standard glassware in combination with magnetic stirrer bars in case of batch reactions,

(ii) time consuming synthesis and characterization procedures that hamper the derivation of

larger datasets and  (iii) the human factor that severely affects reproducibility. Especially  if the

latter is questionable or cannot be sufficiently assured,  it is impossible to discriminate real

physico-chemical effects from experimental noise. Finally, (iv) “dispersity” imposes that not only

the correct material but the correct material with the required particle size distribution (PSD),

shape (distribution), composition and, at least for nanoparticles, surface properties [14], [15]

needs to be produced. This  is leading to an increased degree of complexity as multiple

dimensions in terms of feed composition and process parameters, have to be addressed.[16] An

answer to this multidimensional challenge is the use of automation in a setup that allows a

systematic variation of process parameters to clarify e.g. the impact of mixing on the dynamic

evolution of dispersity. This is expected to be important for developing future scale up rules.

                                      3Automation was successfully implemented in several fields including catalyst development,[17]

optimization of paints[18] and polymers[19] as well as biotechnology.[20] However, very few

platforms for liquid phase batch synthesis of nanomaterials are available.[21] Most notably,

Chan et  al. reported a pioneering study where they implemented an automated platform

(Workstation for Automated Nanomaterial Discovery and Analysis, WANDA) that was used for

deriving an optimum chemistry and synthesis temperature for CdSe QDs by hot injection,

however still very close to the usually used laboratory approach (synthesis in small glass vials

with magnetic stirrer bars).

Although some QD synthesis routes use at room temperature in aqueous solution do exist,[22-

24] hot injection which is focused in here involves the fast addition of a cold precursor (at

~25 °C) to a hot metal-organic precursor (typically at temperatures >225 °C), enabling the

separation of nucleation and growth processes.[25, 26] Thus, so-called nearly monodisperse

products with high crystallinity are obtained.[27] However, especially within the first minute,

particle growth is fast and optical properties change rapidly. This is challenging with respect to

sampling time as well as sampling frequency, especially  if several different particle sizes with

varied band gaps are required.  It is also obvious that the production of such a high-quality

product by hot injection requires highly skilled experimentalists due to (i) high temperatures and

pronounced temperature gradients, (ii) sensitivity of QD syntheses against smallest changes in

feed quality and reactant concentrations, (iii) fast kinetics, (iv) demanding requirements in terms

of cleanliness and the (v) additional need to exclude oxygen and humidity.

that comprises a liquid handling tool, rack holders for various vials and plates, six feed vessels

as well as six stainless steel reactors that can be operated in parallel. In contrast to the usually

used comparatively simple magnetic stirrer bars, our setup is operated with triple blade stirrers

Most relevant evidence (with ids):

## pqac-00000037

From text 'reding2018metaldustexplosion pages 3-4'.

Nicholas S. Reding and Mark B. Shiflett. Metal dust explosion hazards: a technical review. Industrial & Engineering Chemistry Research, 57:11473-11482, Aug 2018. URL: https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.iecr.8b02465, doi:10.1021/acs.iecr.8b02465. This article has 53 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt indicates that NFPA 484 imposes more specialized controls for combustible metal particulates than the general housekeeping provisions of NFPA 654. In particular, water-based cleaning should be avoided where alkali or highly reactive metal dusts are present because even trace moisture can create hazards. Prevention programs should control open flames, hot surfaces, self-heating or smoldering deposits, exothermic decomposition, mechanical-impact sparks, electrical failures, and electrostatic discharge; grounding and intrinsically safe electrical equipment are identified as important safeguards. The excerpt does not provide numerical minimum ignition energy (MIE) or minimum explosible concentration (MEC) values for aluminum, magnesium, or silicon powders, so those values cannot be established from this passage. It does explain that lower oxygen concentration increases the MIE and can eventually prevent sustained flame propagation when the limiting oxygen concentration is reached. Gas blanketing or inerting reduces explosion risk by replacing or diluting oxygen, thereby preventing an explosive atmosphere or making ignition require more energy. Nitrogen is generally suitable for aluminum, whereas argon or helium may be needed for magnesium. Inerting has practical limitations, including cost, personnel-asphyxiation hazards, gas compatibility, leakage, and possible ineffectiveness in large dust-storage volumes. Silicon-specific requirements and numerical MIE/MEC data are not included.

From text 'reding2018metaldustexplosion pages 2-3'.

Nicholas S. Reding and Mark B. Shiflett. Metal dust explosion hazards: a technical review. Industrial & Engineering Chemistry Research, 57:11473-11482, Aug 2018. URL: https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.iecr.8b02465, doi:10.1021/acs.iecr.8b02465. This article has 53 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt identifies NFPA 484 as requiring a more refined housekeeping approach for combustible metal particulate than the general organic-dust guidance in NFPA 654. It specifically states that water-based cleaning should be avoided in areas exposed to alkali or highly reactive materials, while NFPA 654 addresses cleaning frequency, methods, and portable vacuum requirements. The passage also explains the basis for inerting enclosed metal-dust processes: nitrogen, carbon dioxide, or conditioned flue gas can reduce oxidant availability and quench combustion oxidation reactions. Inert-gas systems must be designed to keep oxygen or oxidant concentrations below the level needed for flame propagation, even when the other explosion-pentagon conditions are present. The required oxygen limit depends on both the ignition energy and the particular fuel. This excerpt does not provide the requested numerical minimum ignition energy (MIE), minimum explosible concentration (MEC), or limiting-oxygen/inerting values for aluminum, magnesium, or silicon powders. It also does not specifically discuss argon blanketing, so those metal-specific values and any comparison of argon with nitrogen must be obtained from later sections of the review or the applicable NFPA 484 provisions and test data.

## pqac-00000039

From text 'taveau2019metaldustsexplosion pages 1-2'.

J. Taveau, S. Lemkowitz, S. Hochgreb, and D. Roekaerts. Metal dusts explosion hazards and protection. Chemical engineering transactions, 77:7-12, 2019. URL: https://doi.org/10.3303/cet1977002, doi:10.3303/cet1977002. This article has 24 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt provides background relevant to NFPA 484 combustible-metal-dust safety, but it does not reproduce NFPA 484 requirements or give minimum explosible concentrations (MECs) and inerting limits for aluminum, magnesium, or silicon. It identifies aluminum and magnesium as extremely reactive metals, silicon as highly reactive, and indicates that metal-dust hazard severity depends on reactivity, particle size, and oxide films. Aluminum is described as potentially St3, with KSt greater than 300 bar·m/s, Pmax greater than 10 bar, and MIE below 10 mJ. These values illustrate why robust prevention and protection are needed. The excerpt also cautions that inert atmospheres cannot automatically be assumed safe: many fine and most ultrafine metal powders may burn in carbon dioxide, water vapor, and even nitrogen. Thus, argon or nitrogen blanketing may reduce oxygen-driven ignition or combustion only when the atmosphere is demonstrated to remain below the applicable limiting oxygen concentration and compatible with the specific powder; the text supplies no numerical oxygen, MEC, or inerting criteria. It further states that preventive measures rarely eliminate explosions completely, so explosion-protection measures generally also need consideration.

From text 'reding2018metaldustexplosion pages 4-5'.

Nicholas S. Reding and Mark B. Shiflett. Metal dust explosion hazards: a technical review. Industrial & Engineering Chemistry Research, 57:11473-11482, Aug 2018. URL: https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.iecr.8b02465, doi:10.1021/acs.iecr.8b02465. This article has 53 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt does not provide the NFPA 484 safety requirements, nor does it give numerical minimum ignition energy (MIE) or minimum explosible concentration (MEC) values for aluminum, magnesium, or silicon powders. It does provide limited information about inerting metal dusts. One cited study used minimum inerting criteria of MIE greater than 1000 mJ and minimum autoignition temperature (MAIT) greater than 450 °C. Under those criteria, calcium carbonate effectively inerted iron-alloy and iron–aluminum-alloy dust at 50 wt% and aluminum-alloy dust at 75 wt%; however, it did not sufficiently increase MIE or MAIT for pure atomized aluminum, pure atomized magnesium, or Mg–Al alloy dust. The review therefore characterizes aluminum and magnesium as highly reactive and difficult to inert. It also notes that inertants can work thermally by absorbing combustion heat and chemically by interfering with combustion kinetics, capturing free radicals, and impeding flame propagation. The excerpt does not discuss argon or nitrogen blanketing, oxygen-limit criteria, or how inert atmospheres quantitatively reduce explosion risk. It also contains no silicon-specific MIE, MEC, or inerting data. Those requested values and requirements must therefore be obtained from NFPA 484 and the relevant experimental safety literature, rather than this excerpt.

{"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a decision-matrix table comparing the three glovebox procurement options for the BYU autonomous materials lab. The three options are:
(a) Purpose-built automation-ready glovebox (e.g., LC Technologies LC-100/LC-180, $34K-$50K, or custom-built like A-Lab GPSS)
(b) Retrofit a used purifier-equipped glovebox with internal robot arm (MBraun MB200MOD ~$12K, Vigor SG1200-750TS ~$14K, or refurbished Labconco ~$28K)  
(c) External robot arm + automated antechamber only (arm outside, any glovebox including $3K purge-only Labconco upgraded later)

Compare on columns: Capital Cost, Atmosphere Integrity (sub-ppm O2/H2O), Data Quality for Reactive Powders, Purifier Contamination Risk, Robot Maintenance Complexity, Scalability/Modularity, and Recommended For. Include notes on key trade-offs."}
function.name: create_artifact

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-01)

| Option | Capital cost | Atmosphere integrity: sub-ppm O₂/H₂O | Data quality for reactive powders | Purifier-contamination risk | Robot-maintenance complexity | Scalability / modularity | Recommended for / key trade-off |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **(a) Purpose-built automation-ready glovebox** — LC Technologies LC-100/LC-180 or a custom A-Lab-GPSS-style enclosure | **$34K–$50K quoted for LC box**, before robot, dosing equipment, engineered powder controls, and custom integration. Highest initial cost but lowest retrofit uncertainty. | **Best prospect.** Specify guaranteed loaded performance—not merely an empty-box acceptance test—of ≤1 ppm O₂ and H₂O, adequate recirculation, automated pressure control, analyzers, interlocked load-lock, and recovery testing. Custom double-glovebox precedent shows that floor-mounted arms, a transfer rail, and densely integrated powder-processing stations are feasible (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002). | **Highest potential.** Purpose-designed geometry, stable atmosphere, grounded dosing station, local powder capture, and integrated balance isolation minimize uncontrolled environmental and transfer variables. A-Lab GPSS demonstrates automated air-free powder dispensing, mixing, heating, grinding, and sample preparation, although some characterization remained manual for robustness and cost (pqac-00000002). | **Medium unless explicitly controlled.** Internal robots and powder dosing increase dust, lubricant, polymer-vapor, and furnace-off-gas loading. Require local source capture, replaceable prefilters ahead of the purifier, segregated “dirty” processing, sealed powder containers, and differential-pressure monitoring. | **Medium–high, but designable.** Purchase removable floor plates, glove-port reach to service points, spare feedthroughs, lifting/removal provisions, thermal monitoring, and an isolation/service vestibule. Put controllers, power supplies, PCs, and other high-heat/high-outgassing components outside wherever possible. Dense glovebox layouts otherwise make collisions and service access difficult (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000027). | **High if specified initially.** Extra penetrations, blanked KF/ISO ports, removable work decks, rail provisions, automated antechamber, Ethernet/fiber, 24/48-VDC and AC feedthroughs, and independent powder and clean zones support later expansion. Vertical stacking and sidewall placement of frequently serviced modules are proven space-saving strategies (pqac-00000002). | **Preferred for BYU if true unattended internal powder processing is the objective.** Select this only after a vendor accepts an automation-and-metal-powder user-requirements specification, conducts a loaded factory/site acceptance test, and supports NFPA/AHJ review. It provides the strongest atmosphere and data-integrity foundation but does not by itself make a standard robot or glovebox compliant for combustible metal dusts. |
| **(b) Retrofit a used purifier-equipped glovebox with an internal arm** — MBraun MB200MOD (~$12K), Vigor SG1200-750TS (~$14K), or refurbished Labconco Protector + AtmosPure (~$28K) | **Lowest-to-moderate box price**, but total installed cost can approach a new system after purifier regeneration/repacking, analyzers, leak repair, feedthroughs, reinforced floor, controls, arm installation, guarding, filters, and commissioning. Reserve a substantial contingency. | **Potentially high, but condition-dependent.** A sound recirculating purifier can achieve sub-ppm operation; require helium leak testing, analyzer calibration, glove/seal replacement, purifier-capacity and regeneration verification, and a loaded recovery test before acceptance. An MBraun enclosure has published precedent for an automated Chemspeed workstation, but the paper does not identify its glovebox model or arm installation details (pqac-00000026). | **Potentially high after qualification.** Existing chamber dimensions, vibration, airflow over the balance, inaccessible corners, and residual contamination can introduce batch effects. Establish blank runs, witness coupons, O₂/H₂O time-series logging, gravimetric control charts, and powder carryover tests before scientific use. | **Highest of the three options.** Retrofitted arm gearboxes, cables, plastics, greases, and open powder operations share the recirculation loop with molecular sieve and oxygen-removal media. Fine Al/Mg/Si dust is also an ignition and cross-contamination hazard; aluminum dust can have MIE below 10 mJ, and grounding, ignition-source control, and powder-specific inerting validation remain necessary (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000039). | **Highest.** The arm may not fit through the antechamber, and major service can require opening and repurging the box. Legacy floors may need structural reinforcement; ports may be poorly located; drawings, spare parts, and PLC access may be unavailable. Avoid unless the arm can be removed in modules through a service port or isolated vestibule. | **Medium–low.** Economical for a fixed workflow if chamber depth, ceiling clearance, purifier flow, antechamber size, payload, reach, and collision envelope are already adequate. Retrofitting penetrations or enlarging the chamber can eliminate the initial savings. | **Recommended only as a staged engineering platform after a favorable inspection.** Of the used choices, prefer the unit with documented purifier health, supported controls, adequate chamber volume and service access—not simply the lowest purchase price. A used MBraun or Vigor can be attractive, but reject any unit that cannot pass loaded atmosphere, leak, grounding, and powder-containment acceptance tests. |
| **(c) External robot plus automated antechamber/load-lock** — robot remains in air; internal dosing machine operates in the glovebox | **Potentially lowest-risk staged purchase.** A $3K purge-only Labconco is inexpensive, but purifier, analyzers, vacuum hardware, automated doors/valves, controls, and safety interlocks are additional; the external arm is also additional. A purge-only box should not be budgeted as a sub-ppm production system until upgraded and validated. | **High with a purifier-equipped box and validated vacuum/purge recipe; inadequate for demanding work with purge-only operation.** Interlocked doors and pressure/O₂/H₂O permissives prevent operator shortcuts. Published transfer systems demonstrate transition chambers, glovebox networks, vacuum holders, and automated docking, but quantitative gas use and sub-ppm excursions are rarely reported (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033). | **High for internal dosing if samples remain sealed during external handling.** External robotics avoids adding arm-derived heat and contaminants to the analytical environment. Data quality depends on repeatable carrier geometry, sealed containers, barcode/LIMS custody, and logging of chamber pressure and O₂/H₂O for every transfer. | **Lowest robot-related risk.** The arm, gearbox, belts, lubricants, and most cables stay outside the recirculation loop. Powder can still contaminate the purifier, so use capped vessels, local filtration, spill trays, and a “dirty” transfer vestibule. | **Lowest.** Robot service does not disturb the glovebox atmosphere. The critical maintenance items become door seals, valves, vacuum pump, carrier alignment, and interlock sensors. A published automated vacuum carrier achieved docking in under 60 s, although that result is not a glovebox sub-ppm purge-cycle specification (pqac-00000031). | **Highest modularity for phased development.** External arms can serve multiple stations, carriers can be standardized, and the glovebox can later receive an internal compact manipulator. Throughput is limited by load-lock cycling and by the need for an internal mechanism—or human glove operation—to move carriers between the chamber and dosing station. | **Best near-term risk-adjusted architecture for BYU.** Buy a sound purifier-equipped enclosure—or add a qualified purifier before reactive work—install the powder doser internally, and automate sealed-carrier transfer with the arm outside. This sacrifices fully unattended internal manipulation but minimizes purifier contamination, thermal/outgassing uncertainty, and atmosphere-breaking robot maintenance. Do **not** rely on the $3K purge-only box for quantitative Al/Mg/AlSi10Mg studies until sub-ppm performance and combustible-powder safeguards are demonstrated. |


*Table: Risk-adjusted comparison of purpose-built internal automation, retrofitting a used purifier glovebox, and keeping the robot outside with automated transfer. The matrix separates advertised purchase price from the atmosphere, contamination, maintenance, and combustible-powder controls that will determine total project risk.*

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
